ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The local ethics committee [blinded] approved the present study.
table.formatted: The local ethics committee <ref type="bibr">[blinded]</ref> approved the present study.

table.text: The project was performed in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki and the APA ethical principles.

In a 3×2-mixed online experiment, N = 343 participants were presented either with posts by (i) human greenfluencers, (ii) human-controlled virtual greenfluencers, or (iii) AIcontrolled virtual greenfluencers.
Adult participants (≥18 years) were recruited from the general German population through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com).
table.formatted: Adult participants (≥18 years) were recruited from the general German population through Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com">https://www.prolific.com</ref>).

table.text: Gender was defined via socially constructed roles rather than biological attributes, and participants were asked to indicate which gender they identify with.
Participants provided their electronic informed consent before participation.
First, participants completed self-report measures on socio-demographics and trust (see information in the "Measures" section).
The posts presented to participants were manipulated based on a 3×2-mixed-betweenwithin-subjects survey experiment.

The between-subjects experimental factor was greenfluencer type with three levels: The participants were told that all posts they were presented with were either from (i) virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) human greenfluencers (HG).
Participants assigned to the VG-AI and VG-H conditions were fully debriefed regarding this deception following completion of the experimental procedure.
Following exposure to each post, participants completed ratings of post credibility and self-reported likelihood of engagement, i.e., engagement intentions (see "Measures" section).
A total of N = 444 individuals started participation and provided informed consent.
An additional n = 4 participants were removed because they did not reach the final page of the survey, indicating early termination.

No remaining participants completed the survey more than once, had missing data in variables of interest, or exhibited clear indicators of careless responding (i.e., providing the same response across all items of at least one of the two trust scales).
However, n = 2 participants were excluded because they did not identify as either man or woman, which was an important categorization for the gender congruency analyses.
Finally, n = 67 participants were removed from the data set because they responded incorrectly to a manipulation check item.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: The Psychological Basis of Different Reactions to Posts by Human and Virtual Greenfluencers
table.research_questions:
Hypotheses on Greenfluencer Type and Gender Congruency Between Greenfluencers and Individual: 

H1: Information in posts by HG is rated as more credible than information in posts by VG-H, which is, in turn, rated as more credible than information in posts by VG-AI. [Main effect of Greenfluencer type]

H2: Information in posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, and VG-AI) of the same gender as oneself is rated as more credible than information in posts by Greenfluencers of the other genders. [Main effect of gender congruency]

H3: Information in posts by HG of the same gender as oneself is rated as most credible, whereas information in posts by VG-AI of another gender are rated as least credible. The rating of the credibility of posts by HG of another gender, by male and female VG-H, and by VG-AI of the same gender fall in between. [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and gender congruency]


Regarding main effects of Greenfluencer type and gender congruency, as well as their interaction effects on engagement behaviors (i.e., liking, sharing, and commenting), the expected directions of effects cannot be specified a priori. The existing literature is scarce, heterogeneous and, in part, yields contradictory findings. For example, prior research indicates that higher perceived credibility of a stimulus (e.g., a social media post) is positively associated with engagement outcomes such as sharing (Millet et al., 2024), suggesting effect directions analogous to those hypothesized for credibility. In contrast, other studies report that virtual influencers receive more likes and comments per post than human influencers (Arsenyan & Mirowska, 2021), implying a potentially opposing pattern of effects, at least with respect to the main effect of Greenfluencer type, relative to credibility-based expectations.
For gender congruency effects, while research in marketing contexts – particularly on sponsored content – suggests that gender congruency between influencer and audience can enhance engagement (Hudders & De Jans, 2022), consistent with social identity theory, empirical evidence in the specific context of virtual Greenfluencers is currently lacking.
In light of the absence of a sufficiently developed theoretical framework and the limited, inconsistent empirical evidence, we refrain from formulating directional hypotheses. Instead, we address these relationships through exploratory research questions:

RQ1: How does the engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts differ between posts by HG, VG-H, and VG-AI?

RQ2: How does the engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts differ between posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) that are of the same gender as oneself versus of another gender?

RQ3: What are the interaction effects of Greenfluencer type (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) and gender congruency on engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts?




Hypotheses on Trust in Humans and AI (in Interaction with Greenfluencer Type):

H4: Trust in humans is positively related to credibility ratings of posts by HG, but unrelated to credibility ratings of posts by VG-AI. The relation with credibility ratings of posts by VG-H is unclear. [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in humans]

H5: Trust in AI is positively related to credibility ratings of posts by VG-AI, but unrelated to credibility ratings of posts by VG-H and HG. [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in AI]

No main effects of trust in humans or AI on the general credibility ratings of posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) is expected.


RQ4: What is the relation between trust in humans and engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts of HG, VG-H, and VG-AI? [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in humans]

RQ5: What is the relation between trust in AI and engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts of HG, VG-H, and VG-AI? [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in AI]

No main effects of trust in humans or AI on the general engagement with posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) is expected.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.q5: While the participants do not know the exact experimental conditions before participation, immediately prior to entering the experimental condition, they are informed about the specific condition to which they are assigned, i.e., whether they will be shown posts by (i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG; between-subjects experimental factor with three levels), as well as whether the posts are from a Greenfluencer depicting a (i) woman or (ii) man (within-subjects experimental factor with two levels).
table.study_design_overview:
Two factorial, 3x2-mixed-between-within-subjects survey experiment:
-	Between-subjects experimental factor: Greenfluencer type (three levels: Posts are from (i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG))
-	Within-subjects experimental factor: Depicted gender of the Greenfluencer (two levels: (i) woman, (ii) man / the same or the other gender compared to one's own gender, accordingly).
table.randomization:
Participants are randomly assigned to one of the three experimental conditions of the between-subjects factor (Greenfluencer type; three levels: posts are from (i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG)). Within each condition, participants are presented with posts by a Greenfluencer depicting a man and a Greenfluencer depicting woman (within-subjects factor), whereby the order of the posts by male and female Greenfluencers is randomized; and, within each gender condition, the order of the individual posts is randomized.
All randomizations are conducted by the Unipark (https://www.unipark.com/en/) platform, on which the study is programmed such that an equal number of participants are randomized into each of the three Greenfluencer type experimental conditions and that, across the sample, the order of posts by Greenfluencers depicting a man versus a woman first/second is balanced (50:50) and all possible orders of posts within the respective Greenfluencer gender condition (man vs. woman) are presented (as far as possible) equally often.

table.data_collection_procedures:
Recruitment Strategy:
-	Data will be collected online via the Unipark platform (https://www.unipark.com/en/)
-	The sample will be recruited via Prolific (https://www.prolific.com) 

In-/Exclusion Criteria for Participation:
-	Individuals who are at least 18 years old, provide informed consent, and understand the German language at a native-level proficiency will be allowed to participate
-	No additional in- or exclusion criteria for participation will be set for participation
-	However, participants who attempt to participate when their respective gender quota (50:50 men:women) is full will not be able to participate
-	Additionally, participants who fail two or three out of the three attention check items will be excluded from the analyses
-	Similarly, participants who state that they would not use their own data in a quality check item will be excluded from the analyses
-	Moreover, participants who are identified as speeders (exceptionally fast submissions based on the prolific system + participants with a participation time < 20% of median participation time) will be excluded from the analyses

Sample composition:
-	The sample will consist of individuals from the general adult German population (18+)
-	Quotas for gender will be set 50:50 (which is also close to the distribution of males and females based on German census data)
-	A wide distribution of education levels and federal states of residence is targeted

Incentive for participation:
-	Individuals recruited via Prolific will receive a monetary payment considering minimum wage and the time needed to complete the survey

Timeline:
-	Data collection will take place in February and March 2026
table.sample_size: N = 400 + 5% to account for data cleaning
table.sample_size_rationale:
For a first approximate estimate of the necessary sample size, we conducted a power analysis in G*Power. Using the F test family and, specifically, the “ANOVA: Repeated measures, within-between interactions” model, we set the following parameters: Effect size f = 0.1 (small according to Cohen (1992)), alpha error probability = 0.05, power = 0.80, number of groups = 3, number of measures = 2, correlation among repeated measures = 0.3, and nonsphericity correction = 1. This led to a total necessary sample size of N = 342. However, G*Power and the model we used do not reflect the whole multi-level model we are planning to run since covariates cannot be included. 

Thus, we also conducted a simulation-based power analysis using the simr package in R.
We specified the multilevel model we aim to run in the final analysis and set the fixed effects to small-to-medium. We then compared models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of the experimental conditions, as well as models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of gender congruency. Specifically, we computed a power curve for sample sizes of N = 400 (as we assumed that a larger sample than N = 342 would be required based on the G*Power results), N = 500, N = 600, N = 700, N = 800, N = 900, and N = 1,000.

For the models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of the experimental conditions, a power exceeding 0.80 was already achieved at N = 400. For the models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of gender congruency, a sample size of N = 800 was required to exceed a power of 0.80.

Based on these analyses, and taking into account costs, feasibility, and the fact that exact power analyses are difficult given the largely unknown effect sizes for most effects under investigation, we decided to recruit N = 400 participants, plus an additional 5% over-recruitment to account for data cleaning.

If, based on the effect sizes observed, we have to assume that a larger sample would have been necessary to detect the effects, we may recruit a replication sample. However, we leave this decision open and will report on this issue transparently in the final manuscript.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will be stopped as soon as N = 400 (+5%) participants were recruited.
table.manipulated_variables:
All participants are presented with ten stimuli, i.e., posts. As such, each stimulus is designed as a screenshot showing a post in the style of an Instagram post (viewed on a computer) consisting of a picture, a text, and the usual design elements (e.g., a comment field in which users can write a comment, a like button). No information about the name of the Greenfluencer, no profile picture, and no information on the number of likes, shares, or similar engagement indicators is provided to prevent potential confounding effects.

Between participants, one experimental factor with three levels is manipulated: Greenfluencer type:
(i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI: the Virtual Greenfluencers are completely controlled by AI in that both text in posts as well as pictures are created by generative AI)
(ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H: the Virtual Greenfluencers are controlled by humans in that the text in posts is human written and pictures are created by humans using controlled generative AI)
(iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG: the Greenfluencers are real humans; text in posts is human written and pictures are of real humans)
Thus, participants are told that the five posts by the male and the female Greenfluencer (i.e., ten posts in total) are each from one of the three Greenfluencer types. In reality, and unknown to the participants, all participants see the same ten posts, which are original posts from human Greenfluencers. However, in experimental conditions (i) and (ii) (VG-AI, VG-H), the pictures were modified using ChatGPT by the researchers to present a virtual character, and participants are told that the posts presented to them are from Virtual Greenfluencers (VG-AI or VG-H, respectively).

In addition, within participants, the gender of the Greenfluencers is manipulated such that each participant is presented with five posts by a Greenfluencer depicting a man and five posts by a Greenfluencer depicting a woman in randomized order (order of posts by Greenfluencers’ (man vs. woman) randomized, and within each gender condition the order of individual posts is randomized).
After being presented with each post, participants are asked to rate the perceived credibility of the information in the post as well as the likelihood that they would like, share, and comment on the respective post on social media.

table.title: The Psychological Basis of Different Reactions to Posts by Human and Virtual Greenfluencers
table.research_questions:
Hypotheses on Greenfluencer Type and Gender Congruency Between Greenfluencers and Individual: 

H1: Information in posts by HG is rated as more credible than information in posts by VG-H, which is, in turn, rated as more credible than information in posts by VG-AI. [Main effect of Greenfluencer type]

H2: Information in posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, and VG-AI) of the same gender as oneself is rated as more credible than information in posts by Greenfluencers of the other genders. [Main effect of gender congruency]

H3: Information in posts by HG of the same gender as oneself is rated as most credible, whereas information in posts by VG-AI of another gender are rated as least credible. The rating of the credibility of posts by HG of another gender, by male and female VG-H, and by VG-AI of the same gender fall in between. [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and gender congruency]


Regarding main effects of Greenfluencer type and gender congruency, as well as their interaction effects on engagement behaviors (i.e., liking, sharing, and commenting), the expected directions of effects cannot be specified a priori. The existing literature is scarce, heterogeneous and, in part, yields contradictory findings. For example, prior research indicates that higher perceived credibility of a stimulus (e.g., a social media post) is positively associated with engagement outcomes such as sharing (Millet et al., 2024), suggesting effect directions analogous to those hypothesized for credibility. In contrast, other studies report that virtual influencers receive more likes and comments per post than human influencers (Arsenyan & Mirowska, 2021), implying a potentially opposing pattern of effects, at least with respect to the main effect of Greenfluencer type, relative to credibility-based expectations.
For gender congruency effects, while research in marketing contexts – particularly on sponsored content – suggests that gender congruency between influencer and audience can enhance engagement (Hudders & De Jans, 2022), consistent with social identity theory, empirical evidence in the specific context of virtual Greenfluencers is currently lacking.
In light of the absence of a sufficiently developed theoretical framework and the limited, inconsistent empirical evidence, we refrain from formulating directional hypotheses. Instead, we address these relationships through exploratory research questions:

RQ1: How does the engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts differ between posts by HG, VG-H, and VG-AI?

RQ2: How does the engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts differ between posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) that are of the same gender as oneself versus of another gender?

RQ3: What are the interaction effects of Greenfluencer type (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) and gender congruency on engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts?




Hypotheses on Trust in Humans and AI (in Interaction with Greenfluencer Type):

H4: Trust in humans is positively related to credibility ratings of posts by HG, but unrelated to credibility ratings of posts by VG-AI. The relation with credibility ratings of posts by VG-H is unclear. [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in humans]

H5: Trust in AI is positively related to credibility ratings of posts by VG-AI, but unrelated to credibility ratings of posts by VG-H and HG. [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in AI]

No main effects of trust in humans or AI on the general credibility ratings of posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) is expected.


RQ4: What is the relation between trust in humans and engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts of HG, VG-H, and VG-AI? [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in humans]

RQ5: What is the relation between trust in AI and engagement (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts of HG, VG-H, and VG-AI? [Interaction effect of Greenfluencer type and trust in AI]

No main effects of trust in humans or AI on the general engagement with posts by Greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) is expected.

table.q5: While the participants do not know the exact experimental conditions before participation, immediately prior to entering the experimental condition, they are informed about the specific condition to which they are assigned, i.e., whether they will be shown posts by (i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG; between-subjects experimental factor with three levels), as well as whether the posts are from a Greenfluencer depicting a (i) woman or (ii) man (within-subjects experimental factor with two levels).
table.study_design_overview:
Two factorial, 3x2-mixed-between-within-subjects survey experiment:
-	Between-subjects experimental factor: Greenfluencer type (three levels: Posts are from (i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG))
-	Within-subjects experimental factor: Depicted gender of the Greenfluencer (two levels: (i) woman, (ii) man / the same or the other gender compared to one's own gender, accordingly).
table.randomization:
Participants are randomly assigned to one of the three experimental conditions of the between-subjects factor (Greenfluencer type; three levels: posts are from (i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG)). Within each condition, participants are presented with posts by a Greenfluencer depicting a man and a Greenfluencer depicting woman (within-subjects factor), whereby the order of the posts by male and female Greenfluencers is randomized; and, within each gender condition, the order of the individual posts is randomized.
All randomizations are conducted by the Unipark (https://www.unipark.com/en/) platform, on which the study is programmed such that an equal number of participants are randomized into each of the three Greenfluencer type experimental conditions and that, across the sample, the order of posts by Greenfluencers depicting a man versus a woman first/second is balanced (50:50) and all possible orders of posts within the respective Greenfluencer gender condition (man vs. woman) are presented (as far as possible) equally often.

table.sample_size: N = 400 + 5% to account for data cleaning
table.sample_size_rationale:
For a first approximate estimate of the necessary sample size, we conducted a power analysis in G*Power. Using the F test family and, specifically, the “ANOVA: Repeated measures, within-between interactions” model, we set the following parameters: Effect size f = 0.1 (small according to Cohen (1992)), alpha error probability = 0.05, power = 0.80, number of groups = 3, number of measures = 2, correlation among repeated measures = 0.3, and nonsphericity correction = 1. This led to a total necessary sample size of N = 342. However, G*Power and the model we used do not reflect the whole multi-level model we are planning to run since covariates cannot be included. 

Thus, we also conducted a simulation-based power analysis using the simr package in R.
We specified the multilevel model we aim to run in the final analysis and set the fixed effects to small-to-medium. We then compared models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of the experimental conditions, as well as models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of gender congruency. Specifically, we computed a power curve for sample sizes of N = 400 (as we assumed that a larger sample than N = 342 would be required based on the G*Power results), N = 500, N = 600, N = 700, N = 800, N = 900, and N = 1,000.

For the models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of the experimental conditions, a power exceeding 0.80 was already achieved at N = 400. For the models including versus excluding the main and interaction effects of gender congruency, a sample size of N = 800 was required to exceed a power of 0.80.

Based on these analyses, and taking into account costs, feasibility, and the fact that exact power analyses are difficult given the largely unknown effect sizes for most effects under investigation, we decided to recruit N = 400 participants, plus an additional 5% over-recruitment to account for data cleaning.

If, based on the effect sizes observed, we have to assume that a larger sample would have been necessary to detect the effects, we may recruit a replication sample. However, we leave this decision open and will report on this issue transparently in the final manuscript.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will be stopped as soon as N = 400 (+5%) participants were recruited.
table.manipulated_variables:
All participants are presented with ten stimuli, i.e., posts. As such, each stimulus is designed as a screenshot showing a post in the style of an Instagram post (viewed on a computer) consisting of a picture, a text, and the usual design elements (e.g., a comment field in which users can write a comment, a like button). No information about the name of the Greenfluencer, no profile picture, and no information on the number of likes, shares, or similar engagement indicators is provided to prevent potential confounding effects.

Between participants, one experimental factor with three levels is manipulated: Greenfluencer type:
(i) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI: the Virtual Greenfluencers are completely controlled by AI in that both text in posts as well as pictures are created by generative AI)
(ii) Virtual Greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H: the Virtual Greenfluencers are controlled by humans in that the text in posts is human written and pictures are created by humans using controlled generative AI)
(iii) Human Greenfluencers (HG: the Greenfluencers are real humans; text in posts is human written and pictures are of real humans)
Thus, participants are told that the five posts by the male and the female Greenfluencer (i.e., ten posts in total) are each from one of the three Greenfluencer types. In reality, and unknown to the participants, all participants see the same ten posts, which are original posts from human Greenfluencers. However, in experimental conditions (i) and (ii) (VG-AI, VG-H), the pictures were modified using ChatGPT by the researchers to present a virtual character, and participants are told that the posts presented to them are from Virtual Greenfluencers (VG-AI or VG-H, respectively).

In addition, within participants, the gender of the Greenfluencers is manipulated such that each participant is presented with five posts by a Greenfluencer depicting a man and five posts by a Greenfluencer depicting a woman in randomized order (order of posts by Greenfluencers’ (man vs. woman) randomized, and within each gender condition the order of individual posts is randomized).
After being presented with each post, participants are asked to rate the perceived credibility of the information in the post as well as the likelihood that they would like, share, and comment on the respective post on social media.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  23 installable dependencies detected.
- 2450 statistics stored from the extracted output; 23 of 44 reported tests matched (52.3%).

ethics_statements: The local ethics committee [blinded] approved the present study.
The project was performed in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki and the APA ethical principles.
live_data_statements: In a 3×2-mixed online experiment, N = 343 participants were presented either with posts by (i) human greenfluencers, (ii) human-controlled virtual greenfluencers, or (iii) AIcontrolled virtual greenfluencers.
Adult participants (≥18 years) were recruited from the general German population through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com).
Gender was defined via socially constructed roles rather than biological attributes, and participants were asked to indicate which gender they identify with.
Participants provided their electronic informed consent before participation.
First, participants completed self-report measures on socio-demographics and trust (see information in the "Measures" section).
The posts presented to participants were manipulated based on a 3×2-mixed-betweenwithin-subjects survey experiment.

The between-subjects experimental factor was greenfluencer type with three levels: The participants were told that all posts they were presented with were either from (i) virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) human greenfluencers (HG).
Participants assigned to the VG-AI and VG-H conditions were fully debriefed regarding this deception following completion of the experimental procedure.
Following exposure to each post, participants completed ratings of post credibility and self-reported likelihood of engagement, i.e., engagement intentions (see "Measures" section).
A total of N = 444 individuals started participation and provided informed consent.
An additional n = 4 participants were removed because they did not reach the final page of the survey, indicating early termination.

No remaining participants completed the survey more than once, had missing data in variables of interest, or exhibited clear indicators of careless responding (i.e., providing the same response across all items of at least one of the two trust scales).
However, n = 2 participants were excluded because they did not identify as either man or woman, which was an important categorization for the gender congruency analyses.
Finally, n = 67 participants were removed from the data set because they responded incorrectly to a manipulation check item.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

"OSF_Code_VI_Paper_20260429.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—"
), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: The present paper systematically investigates audience reactions to posts by human greenfluencers versus virtual greenfluencers controlled by humans or AI.

Drawing on persuasion theory and research, we hypothesized that posts by human versus humancontrolled versus AI-controlled virtual influencers and gender-congruent influencers are rated as more credible and that these variables may also be linked to engagement intentions.
Furthermore, we expected that trust in humans and trust in AI are positively related to the perceived credibility of posts of the respective influencer type.
We explored relations with engagement intentions exploratorily.

In a 3×2-mixed online experiment, N = 343 participants were presented either with posts by (i) human greenfluencers, (ii) human-controlled virtual greenfluencers, or (iii) AIcontrolled virtual greenfluencers.
Each participant further saw posts by a greenfluencer depicting (i) a man and (ii) a woman.
Participants self-reported perceived credibility and engagement intentions with each post.
Results show that while gender congruency had no significant effects, participants rated human greenfluencer posts as most credible compared to posts by both virtual greenfluencer types.
Engagement intentions did not differ between greenfluencer types.
Trust in AI emerged as a relevant but nuanced predictor of the different outcomes for different greenfluencer types.
As virtual greenfluencers become more prevalent, differences in reactions to them versus human greenfluencers may attenuate.
Given their scalability, it thus remains important to examine when and for whom virtual greenfluencers and their posts may elicit comparable or even stronger reactions than human greenfluencers.
Social media and the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (gen AI) technologies are fundamentally transforming how people encounter information.
This includes the consumption of politically relevant information.
One of the most striking technological innovations emerging from this convergence is the phenomenon of virtual influencers (VIs).
These are non-human, computer-generated, virtual entities with a large follower base on social media (Bringé, 2022; Byun & Ahn, 2023; Kim & Wang, 2024; The Influencer Marketing Factory, 2022).
text.formatted: These are non-human, computer-generated, virtual entities with a large follower base on social media <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bringé, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Byun & Ahn, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kim & Wang, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">The Influencer Marketing Factory, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Given VIs' complete customizability, controllability, and efficiency in interacting with their audiences, VIs can be strategically engineered and employed to effectively influence audiences at scale in accordance with their operators' goals (Gerrath et al., 2024; You & Liu, 2024).
text.formatted: Given VIs' complete customizability, controllability, and efficiency in interacting with their audiences, VIs can be strategically engineered and employed to effectively influence audiences at scale in accordance with their operators' goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gerrath et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">You & Liu, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, beyond the corporate domain, VIs are increasingly used in political communication and campaigns with potentially far-reaching impacts.

Such use cases include using VIs to communicate on environmental topics, climate change, and sustainability (Lan & Tung, 2024; Tung & Lan, 2024; Wan et al., 2026; You & Liu, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Such use cases include using VIs to communicate on environmental topics, climate change, and sustainability <ref type="bibr">(Lan & Tung, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tung & Lan, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wan et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">You & Liu, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zhang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, empirical research examining the effects of VIs within political domains as well as the psychological basis of such effects remains markedly limited.
With the present study, we therefore address this gap by investigating audience reactions to posts by so-called "greenfluencers".
Greenfluencers are influencers whose messaging centers on topics related to climate change, environmental protection, and sustainability.

Specifically, we systematically examine the effects of influencer type, i.e., different virtual versus human greenfluencers, on two primary outcome variables related to their posts: perceived message/information credibility and likelihood of engagement with the posts.
Furthermore, we consider the role of congruency between the greenfluencer and the individual recipient on the level of humanness and (depicted) gender.
Finally, we also examine the role of individuals' trust in humans and AI on those reactions.
>Theoretical and Empirical Background "Influencers" on social media can generally be understood as accounts with substantial follower bases on social media with the capacity to impact their audience.
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Theoretical and Empirical Background</head> "Influencers" on social media can generally be understood as accounts with substantial follower bases on social media with the capacity to impact their audience.

text.text: Virtual Influencers (VIs) are a novel form of influencers.
They are fictional personas with social media accounts that have large followings on these platforms.
The content featuring VIs is often created with Computer Generated Imagery software, including gen AI capabilities.
VIs also have their own personality and background story, and their appearance can be anthropomorphized to various
There are manifold theories that can inform the derivation of hypotheses in this field.
However, they sometimes offer conflicting predictions regarding potential effects.
A general framework, the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, for instance, indicates that people treat computers or machines as social entities (Nass, 1994; Nass & Moon, 2000).
text.formatted: A general framework, the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, for instance, indicates that people treat computers or machines as social entities <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Nass, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Nass & Moon, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: This paradigm thus suggests broadly comparable reactions to virtual and human greenfluencer posts.
Instead of focusing on such broad frameworks, however, we decided to focus more specifically on theories linked to the dependent variables of the present work, like credibility.
In this context, one important variable that may influence how individuals react to posts by different greenfluencer types is source-recipient congruency; a concept sometimes termed homophily.
Persuasion research demonstrates that source characteristics 1 that align with recipient characteristics increase the persuasive appeal of a message.
Relevant characteristics include both directly observable/physical and not directly observable/psychological variables (Teeny et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Relevant characteristics include both directly observable/physical and not directly observable/psychological variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Teeny et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Given the positive relationship between credibility and persuasion (Hovland & Weiss, 1951), source-recipient congruency can be expected to similarly enhance perceived information credibility.
text.formatted: Given the positive relationship between credibility and persuasion <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hovland & Weiss, 1951)</ref>, source-recipient congruency can be expected to similarly enhance perceived information credibility.

text.text: Moreover, it has been argued that social media platform affordances promote less elaborate cognitive processing (Frauhammer & Dreston, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, it has been argued that social media platform affordances promote less elaborate cognitive processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Frauhammer & Dreston, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This is relevant because social media is the context in which both virtual and human greenfluencers operate.
According to the Elaboration Likelihood Model, less elaborate thinking via the peripheral route increases reliance on heuristic cues (Petty & Brinol, 2012).
text.formatted: According to the Elaboration Likelihood Model, less elaborate thinking via the peripheral route increases reliance on heuristic cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Petty & Brinol, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, source-recipient congruency could serve as a heuristic cue.
As such, congruency may trigger higher credibility perceptions of information in posts from a congruent versus incongruent source.

Empirical evidence supports the proposed effects of source-recipient congruency: research demonstrates that (perceived) similarity between the source and the recipient can increase credibility perceptions of messages like Yelp reviews (Pentina et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence supports the proposed effects of source-recipient congruency: research demonstrates that (perceived) similarity between the source and the recipient can increase credibility perceptions of messages like Yelp reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Pentina et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, these theories and empirical findings lead to the conclusion that on social media, information in posts by entities more similar to oneself is perceived as more credible compared to information in posts from less similar entities.

Applied to the domain of human versus virtual greenfluencers, these arguments suggest that information in posts by human greenfluencers will be perceived as more credible than information in posts from virtual greenfluencers.
This assumption aligns with the 1 and message characteristics and the setting in which a message is presented to the recipient.
uncanny valley hypothesis, particularly when the appearance of virtual greenfluencers is highly human-like (Wang et al., 2015).
text.formatted: uncanny valley hypothesis, particularly when the appearance of virtual greenfluencers is highly human-like <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Wang et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, this prediction is supported by prior findings indicating higher perceived message credibility for posts by human versus virtual influencers in the context of environmental corporate social responsibility communication (Lim et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, this prediction is supported by prior findings indicating higher perceived message credibility for posts by human versus virtual influencers in the context of environmental corporate social responsibility communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Lim et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Another study from outside of the specific greenfluencer context showed that ratings of source credibility were higher for human versus virtual influencers (Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Another study from outside of the specific greenfluencer context showed that ratings of source credibility were higher for human versus virtual influencers <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This further supports the present assumption because source credibility is closely related to message/information credibility ratings (Ou & Ho, 2024).
text.formatted: This further supports the present assumption because source credibility is closely related to message/information credibility ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ou & Ho, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Within the virtual greenfluencer category, operational control mechanisms may introduce an additional source of variance.
Specifically, whether virtual greenfluencers are controlled by humans (VG-H) versus controlled by AI (VG-AI) may differentially affect credibility perceptions.
Virtual greenfluencers controlled by humans retain some similarity to humans in their operational backend.
On the contrary, those controlled by AI represent the greatest ontological divergence from human recipients.
This divergence potentially yields the lowest perceived credibility of information in their posts.
To date, however, empirical research systematically comparing message credibility across these three greenfluencer types (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) is lacking.
In particular, no prior work has distinguished between humanversus AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers.
Beyond source-recipient congruency in terms of ontology/humanness, gender congruency between source and recipient may constitute an additional relevant factor.

Following the same theoretical frameworks and reasoning, information credibility perceptions can be expected to be higher when the greenfluencer (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) is depicted as having the same gender as the recipient.
However, empirical research on gender congruency effects on perceived credibility remains limited, particularly in the (virtual) greenfluencer domain.
Moreover, existing findings on gender congruency effects on credibility from related fields yield heterogeneous results.
Some studies demonstrate positive gender congruency effects on credibility, others report null effects (Newly et al., 2021; White & Andsager, 1991).
text.formatted: Some studies demonstrate positive gender congruency effects on credibility, others report null effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newly et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">White & Andsager, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Yet others report opposing effects (Flanagin & Metzger, 2003).
text.formatted: Yet others report opposing effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Flanagin & Metzger, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, based on the aforementioned frameworks and given the paucity of empirical research on congruency effects within the (virtual) greenfluencer domain, the following preregistered hypotheses are proposed for the present study: H1: Information in posts by HG is rated as more credible than information in posts by VG-H, which is in turn rated more credible than information in posts by VG-AI.

H2: Information in posts by greenfluencers of any type (HG, VG-H, and VG-AI) of the same gender as oneself is rated as more credible than information in posts by greenfluencers of any type of the other genders.
H3: Information in posts by HG of the same gender as oneself is rated as most credible, whereas information in posts by VG-AI of another gender is rated as least credible.
The credibility ratings of posts by HG of another gender, by male and female VG-H, and by same-gender VG-AI fall in between, without a clear hypothesis regarding their relative order.

The existing literature on effects of greenfluencer type and gender congruency on engagement intentions (i.e., liking, sharing, and commenting) remains scarce, heterogeneous, and, in some cases, contradictory.

For example, some prior research indicates that higher perceived credibility of a stimulus (e.g., a social media post) is positively associated with engagement outcomes like sharing (Millet et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, some prior research indicates that higher perceived credibility of a stimulus (e.g., a social media post) is positively associated with engagement outcomes like sharing <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Millet et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings suggest effect directions analogous to those hypothesized for credibility.
In contrast, other studies report that virtual influencers receive more likes and comments per post than human influencers (Arsenyan & Mirowska, 2021; Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In contrast, other studies report that virtual influencers receive more likes and comments per post than human influencers <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arsenyan & Mirowska, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings imply a potentially diverging pattern of effects compared to credibility-based expectations for the main effect of greenfluencer type.

With respect to gender congruency effects, research in marketing contexts (particularly examining sponsored content) suggests that gender congruency between influencer and audience can enhance engagement (Hudders & De Jans, 2022).
text.formatted: With respect to gender congruency effects, research in marketing contexts (particularly examining sponsored content) suggests that gender congruency between influencer and audience can enhance engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hudders & De Jans, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Other research on Instagram interactions more generally finds that especially women tend to interact more with other women than men (Pignolet et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Other research on Instagram interactions more generally finds that especially women tend to interact more with other women than men <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Pignolet et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, empirical evidence in the specific context of virtual greenfluencers is currently lacking.
In light of the absence of a sufficiently developed theoretical framework and the limited, inconsistent empirical evidence, we refrain from formulating directional hypotheses.

Instead, we address these relationships through the following preregistered exploratory research questions 2 : RQ1: How do engagement intentions (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts differ between posts by HG, VG-H, and VG-AI?
text.formatted: Instead, we address these relationships through the following preregistered exploratory research questions 2 : RQ1: How do engagement intentions <ref type="bibr">(liking, sharing, commenting)</ref> with posts differ between posts by HG, VG-H, and VG-AI?

text.text: RQ2: How do engagement intentions (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts differ between posts by greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) that are of the same gender as oneself versus of another gender?
text.formatted: RQ2: How do engagement intentions <ref type="bibr">(liking, sharing, commenting)</ref> with posts differ between posts by greenfluencers (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) that are of the same gender as oneself versus of another gender?

text.text: RQ3: What are the interaction effects of greenfluencer type (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) and gender congruency on engagement intentions (liking, sharing, commenting) with posts?
Individual differences in trust dispositions are likely to impact responses to posts by different greenfluencer types as well.
Attitudinal constructs can be conceptualized through all or some of the following three components: (A) affective, (B) behavioral, and (C) cognitive components (Eagly & Chaiken, 1998).
text.formatted: Attitudinal constructs can be conceptualized through all or some of the following three components: (A) affective, (B) behavioral, and (C) cognitive components <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eagly & Chaiken, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Trust can be seen as a key element within the cognitive components.

Generally, dispositional trust as a personal characteristic of individuals has been defined as follows: "the willingness of a party to be vulnerable to the actions of another party based on the expectation that the other will perform a particular action important to the trustor, irrespective of the ability to monitor or control that other party" (Mayer et al., 1995, p. 712).
text.formatted: Generally, dispositional trust as a personal characteristic of individuals has been defined as follows: "the willingness of a party to be vulnerable to the actions of another party based on the expectation that the other will perform a particular action important to the trustor, irrespective of the ability to monitor or control that other party" <ref type="bibr">(Mayer et al., 1995, p. 712)</ref>.

text.text: Dispositional trust has been theoretically and empirically linked to information evaluation processes.
As such, according to the theoretical framework proposed by Kelton et al. (2008), general trust predispositions are related to the general tendency to trust information.
text.formatted: As such, according to the theoretical framework proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kelton et al. (2008)</ref>, general trust predispositions are related to the general tendency to trust information.

text.text: Trust in information, in turn, is oftentimes seen as encompassing information credibility judgments.
Empirical support for the positive relationship between dispositional trust and trust in information emerges from research on Wikipedia articles.
This relation was additionally mediated by trust in the medium and trust in the source (Lucassen & Schraagen, 2012).
text.formatted: This relation was additionally mediated by trust in the medium and trust in the source <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lucassen & Schraagen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: For the present investigation, it appears theoretically meaningful to distinguish between trust in humans and trust in AI, given the different greenfluencer types of relevance.
No overall main effects of these trust dimensions on aggregate credibility ratings across greenfluencer types (HG, VG-H, VG-AI) are anticipated.

Instead, the theoretical frameworks and empirical findings mentioned before support the following preregistered hypotheses: H4: Trust in humans is positively related to credibility ratings of posts by HG, but unrelated to credibility ratings of posts by VG-AI.
The relation with credibility ratings of posts by VG-H is unclear.

text.text: Adult participants (≥18 years) were recruited from the general German population through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com).
text.formatted: Adult participants (≥18 years) were recruited from the general German population through Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com">https://www.prolific.com</ref>).

text.text: The recruitment targeted a balanced gender distribution (50% women, 50% men).
Gender was defined via socially constructed roles rather than biological attributes, and participants were asked to indicate which gender they identify with.
Participants provided their electronic informed consent before participation.
They received an incentive for complete participation.
Furthermore, they received links to reliable sources for more information on climate change and environmental protection after completion of the study.
We complied with relevant laws and collected data anonymously to ensure data security.
The local ethics committee [blinded] approved the present study.
text.formatted: The local ethics committee <ref type="bibr">[blinded]</ref> approved the present study.

text.text: The project was performed in accordance with the latest revision of the Declaration of Helsinki and the APA ethical principles.
Data collection took place in February 2026.
After data cleaning (see Supplementary Material), the final sample comprised N = 343 participants. n = 178 participants identified as women and n = 165 participants identified as men.
The mean age of the sample was M = 34.41 years (SD = 11.56).

Most participants stated that their highest educational degree was a university (including university of applied sciences) degree (n = 197) or A-level or comparable school leaving certificates (n = 90).
Information on the average time spent on social media can be found in the Supplementary Material.
First, participants completed self-report measures on socio-demographics and trust (see information in the "Measures" section).
Afterward, each participant was presented with ten social media posts.
All posts followed a standardized format designed to resemble Instagram content as viewed on desktop devices.
As such, each post consisted of a picture, accompanying text (i.e., caption), and the usual design elements.
These elements included a comment field and a like button.
To minimize potential confounding variables, posts were presented without greenfluencer identifying information, like the username or profile image.
Engagement metrics such as likes, shares, and comments were also removed.
The stimuli are available from the authors upon reasonable request.
The posts presented to participants were manipulated based on a 3×2-mixed-betweenwithin-subjects survey experiment.

The between-subjects experimental factor was greenfluencer type with three levels: The participants were told that all posts they were presented with were either from (i) virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence (VG-AI), (ii) virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), or (iii) human greenfluencers (HG).
The original German language texts and their English language translations are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

Actually, and unknown to the participants, all participants viewed practically the same stimuli consisting of ten authentic posts originally published by human greenfluencers on Instagram (https://www.instagram.com).
text.formatted: Actually, and unknown to the participants, all participants viewed practically the same stimuli consisting of ten authentic posts originally published by human greenfluencers on Instagram (<ref type="url" target="https://www.instagram.com">https://www.instagram.com</ref>).

text.text: For the VG-AI and VG-H conditions, however, we modified the original images.
For this, we used OpenAI's newest ChatGPT model available between 29 August and 8 September 2025 (https://chatgpt.com) to substitute human figures with virtual characters.
text.formatted: For this, we used OpenAI's newest ChatGPT model available between 29 August and 8 September 2025 (<ref type="url" target="https://chatgpt.com">https://chatgpt.com</ref>) to substitute human figures with virtual characters.

text.text: The modified pictures showed the same individuals but in the style of a virtual persona.
Thus, the virtual greenfluencers were human-like.
Participants assigned to the VG-AI and VG-H conditions were fully debriefed regarding this deception following completion of the experimental procedure.

The within-subjects experimental factor manipulated the depicted gender of the greenfluencer with two levels: each participant was presented with (i) five posts by a greenfluencer depicting a woman and (ii) five posts by a greenfluencer depicting a man.
As mentioned before, these were derived from greenfluencers of the respective gender on Instagram.
Also, the gender of the respective greenfluencer was stated before presenting the posts.
The order of the posts by a greenfluencer depicting a woman versus a man was randomized.
Moreover, within each gender condition, the order of posts by the respective greenfluencer was randomized.
Following exposure to each post, participants completed ratings of post credibility and self-reported likelihood of engagement, i.e., engagement intentions (see "Measures" section).
Dispositional trust in humans and trust in AI were both measured using nine items adapted from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP) trust scale.
This scale assesses constructs corresponding to the NEO-PI-R facet A1: Trust (https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOKey.htm#Trust).
text.formatted: This scale assesses constructs corresponding to the NEO-PI-R facet A1: Trust (<ref type="url" target="https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOKey.htm#Trust">https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOKey.htm#Trust</ref>).

text.text: Thus, in total, each item was administered twice with modified referents: once referencing trust in humans (original wording) and once referencing trust in AI (adapted wording).
One item from the original scale ("Think that all will be well") was excluded.
This is because it could not be unambiguously phrased/attributed to trust in humans or in AI.
Participants responded to all items using a scale ranging from1 = "absolutely disagree" to7 = "absolutely agree".
The items were translated into German by a forward-backward translation procedure by the researchers.
Following reverse-coding of negatively worded items, composite scores were calculated by averaging the answers to the nine items for each trust target (humans, AI).
The internal consistency estimates were Cronbach's alpha = .89 (trust in humans) and Cronbach's alpha = .84 (trust in AI) in the total sample.
Further information on the validity of the rephrased trust in AI scale is provided in the Supplementary Material.
Six items adapted from Hyun Baek et al. (2023), Flanagin and Metzger (2000), and Thiele and Sindermann (2025) were used.
text.formatted: Six items adapted from Hyun <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Baek et al. (2023)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Flanagin and Metzger (2000)</ref>, and Thiele and Sindermann (2025) were used.

text.text: Compared to Thiele and Sindermann (2025), the item on whether the stimuli contained important arguments was removed since it did not fit the present work's context.
Each item was responded to on a scale from1 = "absolutely disagree" to7 = "absolutely agree".
A mean score was computed across the responses to the six items per post.
The internal consistency estimates for the six items per post ranged from Cronbach's alpha = .93 to .97.
Three items were used to ask for the probability that participants would like, share, and comment on each post.
Each item was rated on a scale from1 = "very unlikely" to7 = "very likely".
A likelihood of engagement (short: engagement intentions) score was built across the three items for each post.
The internal consistency estimates for the three items per post ranged from Cronbach's alpha = .81 to .93.

After computing descriptive statistics, the following analyses were conducted to test the hypotheses and explore the research questions: For each dependent variable (perceived credibility, engagement intentions), a multilevel model with the following predictors was computed:

Level 2 (across individuals): two dummy-coded variables on the between-subjects experimental condition of greenfluencer type: (i) VG-AI vs. all others, (ii) VG-H vs. all others (thus, HG was the reference group), and trust in humans and trust in AI.

3   Level 1 (within individuals): the within-subjects experimental factor of gender congruency (0 = incongruent,1 = congruent) between participant and greenfluencer, two interaction effects between greenfluencer type (dummy-coded; see prior explanations) and gender congruency, two interaction effects between greenfluencer type (dummy-coded; see 3 Although no main effects of the trust variables were expected, they were included in the model to test the assumed non-existent effect.
prior explanations) and trust in humans, and two interaction effects between greenfluencer type (dummy-coded) and trust in AI.
We z-standardized all metric variables in the dataset in the long format, and dummycoded categorical variables with 0 and 1.
Further, we set random slopes for individual participants and stimuli, as well as random intercepts for congruency.
We used the lme4 (Bates et al., 2023) and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) packages for these analyses.
text.formatted: We used the lme4 <ref type="bibr">(Bates et al., 2023)</ref> and lmerTest <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref> packages for these analyses.

text.text: Note that the use of the latter was not preregistered.

Finally, in case of significant interactions, we conducted simple slope analyses and pairwise comparisons of slopes, which were not mentioned in the preregistration but are provided for better interpretation of results.

text.text: As can be seen in Table 2 and Figure 1, in both the VG-H and VG-AI groups, the credibility of the posts was rated significantly lower compared to the HG reference group.
text.formatted: As can be seen in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>, in both the VG-H and VG-AI groups, the credibility of the posts was rated significantly lower compared to the HG reference group.

text.text: These findings confirm the first part of H1.
A second (non-preregistered) multilevel model with the VG-AI group as reference was conducted to investigate differences between the two VG groups in credibility ratings.
This model revealed no significant difference between these groups (estimate = 0.11, SE = 0.10, t = 1.11, p = 0.270) in credibility ratings.
This finding is further supported by the rather similar mean perceived credibility scores in both groups shown in Table 1.
text.formatted: This finding is further supported by the rather similar mean perceived credibility scores in both groups shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: This non-significant result does not support the second part of H1.
Also, H2 and H3 on gender congruency effects were not confirmed.
This is due to non-significant main and interaction effects of gender congruency.
Contrary to H4, no significant interaction effects with trust in humans on credibility ratings were observed.
H5, however, was confirmed by a positive effect of the VG-AI by trust in AI interaction effect.
Additionally, the VG-H by trust in AI interaction was significant.

Simple slope analyses revealed a small-to-medium positive slope of 0.23 (SE = 0.07, t = 3.40, p < 0.001, 95%-CI = [0.10;0.37]) in the VG-AI condition, a non-significant slope of 0.07 (SE = 0.07, t = 0.94, p = 0.347, 95%-CI = [-0.07;0.21]) in the VG-H condition, and a small-tomedium negative slope of -0.20 (SE = 0.07, t = -2.90, p = 0.004, 95%-CI = [-0.34;-0.07]) in the HG condition (Cohen, 1992).
text.formatted: Simple slope analyses revealed a small-to-medium positive slope of 0.23 (SE = 0.07, t = 3.40, p < 0.001, 95%-CI = [0.10;0.37]) in the VG-AI condition, a non-significant slope of 0.07 (SE = 0.07, t = 0.94, p = 0.347, 95%-CI = [-0.07;0.21]) in the VG-H condition, and a small-tomedium negative slope of -0.20 (SE = 0.07, t = -2.90, p = 0.004, 95%-CI = [-0.34;-0.07]) in the HG condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cohen, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Pairwise comparisons of the slopes revealed no significant differences between the VG-AI and VG-H slopes (p = 0.098).
However, the slope in the VG-AI condition was significantly higher than in the HG condition (p < 0.001).
text.formatted: However, the slope in the VG-AI condition was significantly higher than in the HG condition (p < 0.001).

text.text: Further, the slope in the HG condition was significantly lower than the one in the VG-H condition (p = 0.007).
Finally, the main effect of trust in AI was also significant and negative. of the effects can be found in Supplementary Figure 1.

text.text: A second, post-hoc (non-preregistered) multilevel model with VG-AI as reference revealed no significant differences between the VG-AI and VG-H conditions either (estimate = -0.03, SE = 0.11, t = -0.26, p = 0.794).
Related to RQ2 and RQ3, no main or interaction effects of gender congruency were observed.
Further, no significant interaction effects with trust in humans were observed (RQ4).
However, significant interactions for trust in AI with both VG-AI and VG-H were observed (RQ5).

Simple slope analyses revealed a small positive slope of 0.17 (SE = 0.08, t = 2.12, p = 0.035, 95%-CI = [0.01;0.32]) in the VG-AI condition, a medium-sized positive slope of 0.29 (SE = 0.08, t = 3.50, p < 0.001, 95%-CI = [0.13;0.45]) in the VG-H condition, and a nonsignificant slope of -0.11 (SE = 0.08, t = -1.31, p = 0.192, 95%-CI = [-0.27;0.05]) in the HG condition (Cohen, 1992).
