text.text: Note.

HG = Experimental group that was presented with posts and informed that those were published by human greenfluencers; VG-H = Experimental group that was presented with posts and informed that those were published by virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by humans; VG-AI = Experimental group that was presented with posts and informed that those were published by virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by Artificial Intelligence.

The present work aimed at investigating perceived credibility ratings and engagement intentions with posts by human greenfluencers (HG), virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by humans (VG-H), and virtual greenfluencers that are controlled by AI (VG-AI).
Additionally, we considered congruency effects between the greenfluencers and recipients in terms of humanness and depicted gender.
Finally, we also examined the role of dispositional trust in humans and AI.
The findings show that posts by human greenfluencers were perceived as more credible than posts by both types of virtual greenfluencers.
There was no difference observed between human-and AI-controlled virtual greenfluencer posts.
These findings partially support H1.

These findings further suggest a categorical distinction between human and virtual greenfluencers: Both virtual greenfluencers controlled by humans and AI seem to be perceived differently from human greenfluencers.
Consequently, both virtual greenfluencer types may have been perceived as dissimilar to the human self.

In line with persuasion research (Teeny et al., 2021), such perception can plausibly explain why the credibility of posts by both virtual greenfluencer types was rated lower than the credibility of the posts by human greenfluencers.
text.formatted: In line with persuasion research <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Teeny et al., 2021)</ref>, such perception can plausibly explain why the credibility of posts by both virtual greenfluencer types was rated lower than the credibility of the posts by human greenfluencers.

text.text: Another pattern emerged for engagement intentions (RQ1) as dependent variable: there were no significant differences in reported engagement intentions for human greenfluencer posts, posts by human-and posts by AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers.
This may be because different effects cancel each other out.
For instance, the advantage in perceived credibility for posts by human greenfluencers may be related to higher engagement intentions with these posts (Millet et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For instance, the advantage in perceived credibility for posts by human greenfluencers may be related to higher engagement intentions with these posts <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Millet et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, however, perceived novelty of virtual greenfluencer posts may increase engagement intentions with their posts as well (Arsenyan & Mirowska, 2021; Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: At the same time, however, perceived novelty of virtual greenfluencer posts may increase engagement intentions with their posts as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arsenyan & Mirowska, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This novelty effect is in line with the argumentation by Stein et al. (2024) for parasocial interactions.
text.formatted: This novelty effect is in line with the argumentation by <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Stein et al. (2024)</ref> for parasocial interactions.

text.text: Further, the absence of differences in perceived credibility and engagement intentions between posts by human-versus AI-controlled virtual influencers is also relevant to highlight.
This lack of differences indicates that the controlling entity is not as relevant for credibility and engagement intention evaluations of posts by virtual greenfluencers.
Other factors of virtual greenfluencers may be more relevant.

Such factors may include anthropomorphism, (perceived) authenticity, and many others as investigated in prior research on virtual influencers in more general contexts (Jiang et al., 2024; Kim & Wang, 2024; H. Lee et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such factors may include anthropomorphism, (perceived) authenticity, and many others as investigated in prior research on virtual influencers in more general contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Jiang et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kim & Wang, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">H. Lee et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: With respect to H2 and H3, as well as RQ2 and RQ3, no main or interaction effects of gender congruency on credibility or engagement intentions were observed.
The absence of main effects aligns with some prior findings, particularly for credibility (White & Andsager, 1991).
text.formatted: The absence of main effects aligns with some prior findings, particularly for credibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(White & Andsager, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Concerning H4 and RQ4, trust in humans was unrelated to both the credibility and the engagement intention outcome.
This was evident in non-significant main effects and interactions of trust in humans with the experimental conditions.
In contrast, trust in AI showed a positive association with credibility ratings.
This relation was most pronounced for posts by AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers.
This finding is in line with H5, and it suggests that greater trust in AI is linked to higher tendencies to believe information in posts by AIcontrolled virtual greenfluencers.
Interestingly, the slopes of the associations of trust in AI and credibility ratings did not differ between the two virtual greenfluencer experimental conditions.
However, looking at each slope individually, the respective slope in the humancontrolled virtual greenfluencer condition was non-significant.
The slope in the human greenfluencer condition was negative.
Trust in AI was also related to engagement intentions in both virtual greenfluencer conditions.
Again, there were no significant differences in the slopes between the two conditions.
Trust in AI was not significantly related to engagement intentions in the human greenfluencer condition (RQ5).
A non-significant or negative association between trust in AI and credibility ratings and engagement intentions with human greenfluencer posts is to be expected.
This is because the introduction to the human greenfluencer experimental condition of the present work did not mention the use of AI.
Thus, other variables may be more relevant to predict credibility ratings and engagement intentions here.
Such variables may include (perceived) entertainment value, attractiveness, and expertise in the context of engagement intentions (Ao et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such variables may include (perceived) entertainment value, attractiveness, and expertise in the context of engagement intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ao et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the positive relations of trust in AI with engagement intentions in the human-controlled virtual greenfluencer condition seem surprising at first.
These findings cannot be explained with certainty at this point.
Nevertheless, one possible explanation for these results is that participants perceived the production of posts by human-controlled virtual greenfluencers as a hybrid process.

Thus, for engagement intentions, trust in AI could support engagement with AI-gereated posts, but most strongly when a human remains accountable; thus, in the humancontrolled virtual greenfluencer condition.
Yet, trust in AI may be less relevant when no human agent is perceived, i.e., in the AI-controlled greenfluencer condition.

Moreover, the smaller, but not significantly different, relation between trust in AI and engagement intentions with AI-versus human-controlled virtual greenfluencer posts could additionally be explained by other factors beyond general trust in AI.
Examples of potentially other relevant variables may be more specifically related to individual virtual greenfluencers.

As such, these variables could include the virtual greenfluencer's interactivity, the emotionality in a virtual greenfluencer's posts, or individuals' trust in a specific virtual greenfluencer (Ju et al., 2024; C. T. Lee & Shen, 2025; Xie-Carson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: As such, these variables could include the virtual greenfluencer's interactivity, the emotionality in a virtual greenfluencer's posts, or individuals' trust in a specific virtual greenfluencer <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Ju et al., 2024</ref>; C. T. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lee & Shen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Xie-Carson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These interpretations are, however, posthoc, cannot be tested with the present data, and thus remain speculative and require further investigation.

Against this background, it is nevertheless important to note that trust in humans and trust in AI were only weakly positively related (r = 0.13, p = 0.014; see Supplementary Material for further a priori validation of the trust in AI scale in a different sample).
Within an emerging but heterogeneous field, the present findings have some relevant theoretical and practical implications.
On a theoretical level, the results on engagement seem to align with the CASA paradigm (Nass, 1994; Nass & Moon, 2000).
text.formatted: On a theoretical level, the results on engagement seem to align with the CASA paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Nass, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Nass & Moon, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The CASA paradigm posits that computers (here: virtual greenfluencers) are perceived as social actors comparable to humans.
Such a similarity in perceptions may explain the lack of differences between the experimental groups found in the present work.
However, since we did not assess participants' perceptions of the social role of the greenfluencers themselves, further research in this direction is needed.
The findings related to credibility seem to be more consistent with the uncanny valley hypothesis (Wang et al., 2015) and congruency effects (Teeny et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The findings related to credibility seem to be more consistent with the uncanny valley hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Wang et al., 2015)</ref> and congruency effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Teeny et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This is because credibility ratings were higher for human compared to both virtual human-like greenfluencers.
The results related to credibility may also be explained via Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner, 2004).
text.formatted: The results related to credibility may also be explained via Social identity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Tajfel & Turner, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: According to this theory, individuals strive to maintain a positive view of their ingroup (Tajfel & Turner, 2004).
text.formatted: According to this theory, individuals strive to maintain a positive view of their ingroup <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Tajfel & Turner, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, messages from sources perceived as similar to oneself (i.e., ingroup members) should be perceived as more credible compared to messages from dissimilar sources representing outgroup members.
However, perceived similarity and identification were not directly tested in the present work.

Thus, while prior work shows that human compared to virtual influencers can achieve higher perceived homophily (Dondapati & Dehury, 2024), both similarity in ontology and (depicted) gender and perceived homophily are not the same.
text.formatted: Thus, while prior work shows that human compared to virtual influencers can achieve higher perceived homophily <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dondapati & Dehury, 2024)</ref>, both similarity in ontology and (depicted) gender and perceived homophily are not the same.

text.text: At the same time, it remains an open question whether the effects on credibility ratings found in the present work will persist as virtual greenfluencers become more embedded in everyday social media environments.
Evidence from other contexts suggests a potential convergence: for instance, Stein et al.
(2024) report no differences in parasocial interactions between human and virtual influencers in a gaming context.
Although not directly comparable, this finding implies that, under certain conditions, perceptions of human and virtual influencers may align.
This pattern may extend to greenfluencers as such agents become increasingly normalized.
As for practical implications, individuals currently appear rather skeptical about the credibility of posts by virtual greenfluencers.
However, greater trust in AI was associated with higher perceived credibility and engagement intentions in the present work.
Thus, with the increasing incorporation of AI into everyday life and social media, trust in AI may increase.
In turn, credibility and engagement intentions with posts by virtual greenfluencers are also likely to increase.
Since greenfluencers are a specific type of political influencers, these effects may generalize to the broader field of virtual political influencers.
As outlined in the introduction, this could have far-reaching consequences, both aligning with and contradicting democratic principles.
This is because virtual (political) influencers, including virtual greenfluencers, can be strategically engineered and employed to leverage human idiosyncrasies in information processing.
Virtual (political) influencers can thereby effectively influence audiences at scale in line with their operators' goals (Gerrath et al., 2024; You & Liu, 2024).
text.formatted: Virtual (political) influencers can thereby effectively influence audiences at scale in line with their operators' goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gerrath et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">You & Liu, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this, operators could further enhance perceived credibility and engagement intentions of the posts through specific design choices.

Such choices may include the use of specific emotions in the posts to improve attitudes toward the virtual in-/greenfluencer (Ham et al., 2024), message warmth (Gerrath et al., 2024), or any other variable related to the appearance, background story, or posts and messages of the virtual in-/greenfluencer.
text.formatted: Such choices may include the use of specific emotions in the posts to improve attitudes toward the virtual in-/greenfluencer <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Ham et al., 2024)</ref>, message warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gerrath et al., 2024)</ref>, or any other variable related to the appearance, background story, or posts and messages of the virtual in-/greenfluencer.

text.text: Thus, knowing how and why virtual greenfluencers and the broader range of other virtual political influencers can impact their recipients can help prevent harmful effects, such as anti-democratic manipulation, and thereby strengthen democratic resilience.
We therefore call for more research into virtual political influencers, going beyond the focus of the present work on virtual greenfluencers.

More specifically, we argue that we are currently at a brief window where the phenomenon of virtual political influencers is advanced enough for rigorous empirical investigation yet early enough for research to educate citizens and advise policymakers before their impacts become irreversible.

Nevertheless, when considering these practical implications, it is important to once again note that the present work focused on a very particular type of virtual political influencers, namely virtual greenfluencers.
Thus, the generalizability of findings must be tested in future studies.
The findings also need to be seen in light of the following limitations.
First, the use of self-report measures may suffer from biases like a lack of interoception.
Furthermore, in the case of engagement intentions, the self-reports did not assess actual engagement behavior but only the likelihood of liking, sharing, and commenting.
Importantly, engagement intentions must be distinguished from actual engagement with posts.

Engagement behavior may not only depend on intentions but also on factors like language style and perceived authenticity, potentially in interaction with source characteristics (Alim et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Engagement behavior may not only depend on intentions but also on factors like language style and perceived authenticity, potentially in interaction with source characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alim et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zheng et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, examining engagement intentions limits the ecological validity of the respective findings of the present work.
Second, the fact that overall, the posts by the female influencer were rated as slightly more credible may have reduced any existing effects of gender congruency.
Third, we only used two greenfluencers as the basis for the experimental stimuli, limiting the generalizability to other influencers and political issue domains.

Fourth, the final sample was smaller than initially intended (N = 400), given thorough data cleaning, including the exclusion of all participants who incorrectly responded to the attention check item.
Fifth, both virtual greenfluencer conditions used the same images with the same virtual avatars.
Only the written introduction in one condition stated that the virtual persona was controlled by humans (VG-H) and in the other condition that it was controlled by AI (VG-AI).

The virtual avatars in the images may have a stronger impact on audience reactions compared to the written information in the introduction to each experimental condition about whether the greenfluencer was human-or AI-controlled.

Nevertheless, given the pretest of the experimental manipulation, the clear presentation and explanations of influencer types, and the focus of the statistical analyses only on participants correctly responding to the manipulation check, we believe we were able to clearly differentiate between the two greenfluencer types.
In conclusion, the present findings shed light on an area of growing promise but also risk: virtual greenfluencers.
Posts by virtual greenfluencers were perceived as less credible than those by human greenfluencers.
Yet, individuals tended to intend to engage similarly with posts by human and both types of virtual greenfluencers. elicited similar engagement intentions.

Furthermore, evaluations of credibility and engagement intentions did not differ between human-and AI-controlled virtual greenfluencers, suggesting that the source of control may be of little relevance to audiences here.
Additionally, trust in AI was positively related to both credibility and engagement intentions with virtual greenfluencers.
These findings lay the basis for further investigations into the psychological basis of reactions to virtual greenfluencers.
Further research should also examine whether these findings generalize to other virtual political influencers given their potentially far-reaching consequences.

text.text: A total of N = 444 individuals started participation and provided informed consent.

Of these, n = 16 were excluded due to not meeting at least one inclusion criterion (minimum age of 18 years; providing consent, native-level proficiency in German) or did not provide information on the respective variables to test the in-/exclusion.
An additional n = 4 participants were removed because they did not reach the final page of the survey, indicating early termination.
To identify potential speeders, we calculated the median completion time among the remaining participants.
Three participants fell below the preregistered threshold of participation time of 20% of the median time; however, each of these cases showed a recorded completion time of -1.
On the Unipark platform, this value indicates interrupted participation rather than unusually rapid responding.
As these participants nevertheless reached the final page and provided complete data, they were retained in the dataset.
Further exclusions were applied as follows: n = 2 participants failed two or more attention check items, and n = 10 indicated that, if they were the researchers, they would not use their own data.
These participants were excluded accordingly.

No remaining participants completed the survey more than once, had missing data in variables of interest, or exhibited clear indicators of careless responding (i.e., providing the same response across all items of at least one of the two trust scales).
However, n = 2 participants were excluded because they did not identify as either man or woman, which was an important categorization for the gender congruency analyses.
Finally, n = 67 participants were removed from the data set because they responded incorrectly to a manipulation check item.

This item asked participants about the influencer type from they were presented posts from (response options: human, human-controlled virtual, AI-controlled virtual), i.e., the experimental condition they were in.
This led to a final sample of N = 343 participants.

The distribution of time spent on social media was as follows: n = 1 participant indicated not using social media at all, n = 137 stated using social media for 0-2 hours per day, n = 139 for 2-4 hours per day, n = 44 for 4-6 hours per day, n = 16 for 6-8 hours per day, n = 5 for 8-10 hours per day, n = 0 for 10-12 hours per day, and n = 1 for 12-14 hours per day.
No participant stated to use social media for a longer time per day.

We decided to adapt an existing, validated trust in humans scale to the AI context to minimize differences in item content and wording that might otherwise contribute to differences in findings between trust in humans and trust in AI.

We tested the adapted items in a pilot study conducted in the realm of a university course led by the senior author of this work (N = 216 after data cleaning; 89 men; Mage = 31.95 years, SDage = 15.91).

Using the data from this pilot study, we first conducted a one-factor confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012) in R. All 18 items assessing trust in humans and trust in AI were modeled to load on one single latent factor.

This model showed poor fit to the data (Comparative Fit Index (CFI) = .512, Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) = .447, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) = .150, Standardized Root Mean Squared Residual (SRMR) = .147).

A two-factor model comprising separate, correlated factors for trust in humans and trust in AI showed substantially improved fit (CFI = .835, TLI = .811, RMSEA = .088, SRMR = .073; χ² difference test: Δχ² = 434.3, p < .001), although several fit indices remained below conventional standards for good model fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999).
